attribution.note: Marcus's own tweet, embedded in his own post and endorsed there.

semantics.note: The wording is faithful. But this is a general truism used as moral framing for 'better choices'. It is rhetorical, not a testable causal claim, so the 'causal' label does not fit.

contract.note: The contract correctly treats the statement as untestable and sets the axis to not_applicable.

reviews.rationale: The statement names no specific choice, consequence, measure or time frame. It works as framing for a normative appeal. No outcome could support or falsify it, so it is not adjudicable. The case itself is not broken.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He cites Time's reporting but asserts the claim himself.

semantics.note: A past-tense observation about OpenAI's outsourced labelling. Marcus's own explanation (Kenya, under $2/hour, toxic content) sets its scope.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'sweatshop' as very low pay, harsh conditions and hidden outsourcing is ordinary and comes from Marcus's own gloss. It is not stretched for or against him.

evidence.note: Time's investigation: OpenAI used outsourced Kenyan workers earning under $2/hour.
Payslip-based take-home pay of about $1.32–$2/hour. OpenAI does not disclose its outsourcers, which fits 'behind the scenes'.
Workers report heavy quotas, traumatic content and mental scarring. This fits harsh conditions.
The contractor disputes the figures, but this is a company disclosure. Even its own range ($1.46–$3.74) is still very low pay, so the contradiction condition is not met.

reviews.rationale: Investigative reporting based on documents and payslips shows outsourced Kenyan labellers paid about $1.32–$2/hour, doing traumatic work under quotas, with the outsourcer undisclosed. Sama's dispute is self-serving and still describes low pay. On the plain reading, the support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. The embedded Hikmet tweet is only his source.

semantics.note: An observation about testimony. 'Apparently' is an evidential qualifier, not a probability hedge, and it is preserved. The 'absolute necessity' aside is expert opinion and is not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'some employees' as at least one senior employee is slightly generous to Marcus but reasonable. Using Elluswamy instead of the Shroff deposition is disclosed and fits 'court testimony this week'.

evidence.note: The Autopilot software head did not know whether the team had human-factors engineers and did not recall any perception-reaction training.
He would have to guess what perception-reaction time means. This fits 'apparently unaware'.
Reuters, Jan 17 2023: shows the witness's seniority and that the testimony was newly reported that week.

reviews.rationale: Testimony made public that week shows the director of Autopilot software unfamiliar with core human-factors concepts and staffing, which meets the support condition. Caveat: only one employee is verified (the plural 'some' is not), and the Shroff deposition could not be checked.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A negative historical observation covering Oct 2016 to Jan 2023, for all cars. Scope and threshold (intervention-free, LA to NYC) are preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. The support and contradiction conditions suit a negative existence claim.

evidence.note: Inverse, Oct 2021: the promised cross-country drive still had not happened. This covers most of the window.
A Dec 2025 'world's first' claim from a Tesla executive. It is a company statement about a later period (and the drive ended in Myrtle Beach), so it is context only, though consistent.
The 2015 Delphi drive predates the window and involved human takeovers.

reviews.rationale: A source from within the period confirms no such drive by Oct 2021, and the packet holds no record of any intervention-free LA–NYC drive before Jan 2023. The support condition is met. Caveat: Oct 2021–Jan 2023 is backed only indirectly, by a later company 'first' claim.
